note: Proposes a benchmark lifecycle covering design, validation, monitoring and retirement, an audit ready framing.
title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Survey of the Science of Evaluation, Benchmarking, and Methodologies for Large Language Models

reading.body:
Popular benchmarks for large language models do not measure what developers and buyers believe they measure, creating systematic misprediction of real-world performance.

The gap between leaderboard scores and actual capability has become a structural problem in AI evaluation. Models that rank highly on standard tests frequently fail in deployment by making errors or producing harmful outputs that the benchmarks never surface. This disconnect arises because evaluation instruments remain static while model behavior evolves, enabling data contamination and gaming of specific metrics. The problem is not merely methodological. It is economic. Organizations making deployment decisions based on published scores face compounded risk: they may select inferior systems, overpay for marginal improvements, or discover after investment that capabilities do not match expectations.

The paper proposes treating evaluation itself as a lifecycle rather than a leaderboard. The framework moves through design of measurement instruments, validation that they measure genuine capability, monitoring performance in use, and retirement when instruments become obsolete or compromised. This systematization matters because it treats benchmarks as tools requiring maintenance rather than permanent facts. Five evaluation approaches emerge from the survey: static benchmarks, dynamic adaptive testing, interactive agentic evaluation, human-in-the-loop methods, and model-based evaluation. Each addresses different aspects of capability but none alone captures what deployed systems must actually do.

The data does not specify which benchmarks failed most severely, which companies suffered material losses from misprediction, or how much compute and infrastructure cost was wasted on models selected through unreliable metrics. It does not measure the performance of the proposed lifecycle framework in practice or compare its cost to current evaluation approaches. These gaps mean the paper identifies a real problem in how AI capability is assessed but cannot quantify its economic impact on the compute and power infrastructure decisions that follow from benchmark-driven model selection.

explain_beginner: This survey asks why AI language models that score extremely well on popular public leaderboards still sometimes fail in embarrassing or even harmful ways once real people start using them, giving wrong answers confidently or producing content nobody wanted. The authors' answer is that the dominant style of testing, a fixed set of questions with fixed correct answers, measures something narrower than real world usefulness or safety, and that models can be tuned to score well on that narrow target without becoming more genuinely reliable, a pattern the paper connects to the well known problem where a model trained on data containing the test questions will score higher than its actual ability. Sheikhi and coauthors organize the different ways researchers currently try to evaluate these systems, from fixed test sets to newer approaches involving live conversation and human judges, and propose a structured lifecycle for building and retiring evaluation tools, so an evaluation method itself gets checked, updated, and eventually replaced rather than treated as a fixed, permanent yardstick. The paper is a synthesis of existing evaluation science, it does not itself introduce a new test that fixes the problems it describes.
explain_business: The core message for any organization relying on public leaderboard rankings to choose or justify an AI model purchase is that a high leaderboard score is a weaker signal of real world reliability than it appears, because the paper documents systematic ways scores get inflated relative to genuine capability, through data contamination and through optimization aimed specifically at leaderboard performance rather than general quality. The Benchmark Lifecycle framework this survey proposes is directly useful as an internal governance checklist, treating any evaluation method an organization relies on, whether public or internally built, as something that needs periodic validation and eventual retirement rather than a one time checkbox at procurement. Since this is a survey rather than a new tool, the business action available right now is process adoption, building an internal habit of re-validating benchmark relevance over time, not waiting on a specific new benchmark the paper does not provide, before treating any leaderboard ranking as sufficient justification for a model choice in a compliance sensitive or safety sensitive deployment.
explain_practitioner: The authors organize existing large language model evaluation approaches into five categories, static benchmarks with fixed question and answer sets, dynamic or adaptive evaluation that adjusts based on model responses, interactive agentic evaluation that tests models acting across multi-step tasks, human in the loop evaluation, and model based evaluation where another AI system grades the outputs, then analyze known failure patterns across all five, particularly data contamination, where benchmark answers leak into training data, and leaderboard gaming, where a model or its prompting is optimized specifically to score well on a public leaderboard rather than to perform better generally. Their central proposed contribution is a Benchmark Lifecycle framework, treating an evaluation benchmark as something with stages, design, validation against known failure modes, deployment monitoring for score inflation over time, and formal retirement once it becomes contaminated or outdated, rather than a fixed artifact used indefinitely. As a survey, the paper's evidence is the breadth and consistency of the problems it documents across the existing literature rather than a new experimental result, and it does not resolve which of the five evaluation approaches is best for a given use case.
